FPMC combines user–item matrix factorization with first-order item transitions. FOSSIL replaces explicit user preference vectors with a normalized sum of historical item embeddings, adding multiple recent-item transitions with global and user-specific lag weights. Its “higher-order” component is an additive combination of pairwise terms; it does not contextualize history items jointly as a Transformer can. These are established baselines for separating long-term preference from recent transitions. [FOSSIL paper](https://arxiv.org/html/1609.09152)

“Do Sequential Recommendation Benchmarks Really Require Higher-Order Sequence Modelling?” finds that SeqRules or PCTM outperform both SASRec/eSASRec reproductions on Amazon Beauty, Sports, Toys and MovieLens-1M, but trail on MovieLens-20M. SeqRules sums distance-weighted transition counts with recency weighting and optional source-item IDF. PCTM uses smoothed transition probabilities, recency-weighted log probabilities, and a separate log-popularity adjustment. Its sparse implementation stores log(1 + count × catalog_size / smoothing), preserving zero-count backgrounds. Evaluation uses full-catalog NDCG@10 with seen-item filtering; these results cannot be transferred directly to RecHarness’s four different categories and 99-negative HR@10 protocol. [Results](https://github.com/spotify-research/sequential-capacity-probes), [formulas and protocol](https://github.com/spotify-research/sequential-capacity-probes/blob/main/docs/PROTOCOL.md)

Inference recommendation: calibration makes popularity comparisons more informative only with matched tuning and ablations—SASRec alone, plus popularity, plus transitions, and plus both. Raw sparse counts and dense logits have incompatible scales; candidate-wise standardization can amplify rare nonzero transitions or depend strongly on sampled candidates. Compare log-compressed transitions and a separately weighted log-popularity residual, fitting scales on validation only. Inspect zero-score frequency, nonzero quantiles, and residual influence per category. This is an experimental recommendation, not an established guarantee that normalization improves HR@10.
